plan:
# Experiment Design: Effect of Period Settings on PDF Performance on ETTm1

## 1. Objective
Quantify how changing the period settings of the PDF (period-decomposition-style) forecasting model changes its forecasting performance on the ETTm1 dataset, isolating the period setting as the sole manipulated factor while everything else is held fixed. No experiment is run or claimed; this document specifies the design that would answer the question.

## 2. Assumed model and operationalization of "period settings" (ASSUMPTION — not source-backed)
Context: the task workspace contains no repository and no dataset (only task.json; track.md states "Design-only task; repositories and compute are not required"), so parameter names and defaults cannot be quoted from code. The following is a stated design assumption.

- Assumed model family: a long-term time-series forecasting model in the Autoformer / Time-Series-Library ecosystem that operates by recovering dominant periodicities from the input (e.g., via FFT/top-k period selection) and then decomposing, segmenting, or grouping the series by those periods before modeling. "PDF" is taken to be such a period-decomposition framework.
- Assumed "period settings": the knobs controlling which periods the model uses. We define a parameterized axis with three sub-components, so that if a concrete repo later exposes a differently-named parameter, that axis swaps in without changing the experiment logic:
  - K: the number of periods used (e.g., top-K from frequency analysis).
  - {P}: the concrete period values used (in samples at ETTm1's 15-min granularity), e.g., daily cycle = 96, half-day = 48, weekly = 672, plus FFT-detected dominant periods.
  - Selection mode: auto (FFT-driven top-K) vs forced/fixed period set.
- Parameterized mapping: the design defines a single abstract independent variable "period setting" = (K, {P}, mode). When the real repository is available, this tuple is bound to that repo's actual period parameters (e.g., whatever names it uses); the experimental logic below is unchanged.

## 3. Dataset and evaluation conventions (ASSUMPTION — standard convention, to be confirmed against repo)
- Dataset: ETTm1 — Electricity Transformer Temperature, 15-minute resolution, 4 channels (e.g., HUFL, HULL, MUFL, MULL), ~69,680 timestamps.
- Split: contiguous time blocks into train / validation / test (library-family convention, e.g., ~12/4/8 months at the 15-min scale); exact borders to be read from the repo when available. No shuffling across time.
- Normalization: per-channel z-score computed on the training split only; applied to val/test with the same statistics; predictions un-normalized back to original scale before metric computation so values are comparable to published tables. (Normalized MSE may be reported as a secondary metric.)
- Input/output format: sliding windows of length seq_len fed to the model; forecast horizon pred_len ∈ {96, 192, 336, 720}. seq_len is held fixed at the repo-default value (assumed 96 or 336) across all runs.

## 4. Independent variable and grid
- Grid over the period-setting axis (K, {P}, mode):
  - Baseline: the repository's default period configuration (whatever it is).
  - K sweep: number of periods ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} (auto selection), default K held elsewhere.
  - Forced-period sweep: concrete period sets relevant to 15-min data, e.g., {96}, {672}, {96,672}, {48,96,672}, and a no-period/"none" ablation where the period machinery is disabled if permitted.
  - Auto vs forced: compare auto top-K against a forced {96,672} set (a direct test of whether auto-selection buys anything).
- One-at-a-time variation: vary exactly one sub-component per run relative to baseline; all other sub-components at default.
- Explicitly NO per-setting hyperparameter tuning: the same optimizer schedule, epochs, and early-stopping rule are applied to every setting. This keeps the period effect causal (a per-setting tuned optimum would confound period effect with tuning effort).

## 5. Dependent variables
- Primary: MSE and MAE per horizon (96, 192, 336, 720) computed over the full ETTm1 test set; plus mean-over-horizons MSE/MAE per setting.
- Secondary (optional): per-channel MSE, normalized MSE, and forecast-time curves, useful for diagnosing which channel/season drives any effect.

## 6. Controls (fixed for every run)
- Data pipeline: same ETTm1 file, same split borders, same normalization, same windowing, same evaluation windows and metric code path (one shared function for MSE/MAE).
- Model: same architecture, same weight-init scheme, same random seed.
- Optimizer/training: same optimizer (e.g., Adam) and learning rate (e.g., repo default lr), same batch size, same training epochs and/or early-stopping criterion on validation MSE (identical patience), same dropout.
- Evaluation: identical test-set evaluation protocol and metric computation; identical hardware/environment for all runs.
- Baseline configuration (default period settings + default hyperparameters) is run as the reference every time so all comparisons are relative to a same-run baseline.

## 7. Analysis plan
1. Main results table: rows = period setting (baseline plus each grid point), columns = horizons {96,192,336,720} and "mean", cells = MSE / MAE.
2. Relative change vs baseline: for each setting and horizon, Δ% = (metric_setting − metric_baseline)/metric_baseline; a per-horizon heatmap or bar chart of Δ%.
3. Short vs long horizon: group horizons {96,192} vs {336,720}; test whether period settings move short-horizon error differently than long-horizon error (e.g., whether long horizons are more sensitive to K or to the forced period set). This directly bears on "does the optimal period configuration grow with horizon".
4. Stability check (optional but recommended): re-run the baseline and 2–3 most informative settings (e.g., K=1, K=5, forced {96,672}) with 3 distinct seeds; report mean±std MSE/MAE per horizon.
5. Noise-vs-effect check (optional): paired comparison across seeds (same seed, differing only in period setting) via paired Wilcoxon signed-rank and/or paired bootstrap CI of the mean difference, to state which differences exceed run-to-run noise.
6. Decision rule: a setting is "better" only if the mean difference and its CI/paired-test support it at the chosen horizon, not just pointwise better.

## 8. Feasibility
- ETTm1 is small (≈70k points, 4 channels, seq_len ≤ 336). On the available 224-core CPU environment with a lightweight forecast model, a single (setting × horizon) run is estimated at minutes to tens of minutes; the full grid (≈6–9 settings × 4 horizons × 1–3 seeds) is tractable on CPU.
- Explicit statement: EXECUTION IS NOT REQUIRED AND WAS NOT PERFORMED for this design-only task; the design would run only if the environment later supplies the repository and data. No numerical results, tables, or plots are claimed.

## 9. Assumptions and uncertainties (all source-dependent claims flagged)
- ASSUMPTION: the identity of "PDF" and that "period settings" = (K, {P}, mode) of a period-decomposition model; the exact named code parameter cannot be verified because no repository exists in the workspace (verified empty).
- ASSUMPTION: ETTm1 uses standard contiguous split, z-score normalization, horizons {96,192,336,720}; exact borders/defaults pending repo.
- ASSUMPTION: repo-default hyperparameters (seq_len, epochs, lr, batch, dropout) form the fixed baseline control.
- ASSUMPTION: performance = MSE/MAE on the test set per horizon.
- ASSUMPTION: one-at-a-time grid with no per-setting tuning is the causal design; interactions (K × {P}) are out of scope as primary.
- UNCERTAINTY: whether auto (FFT) period selection vs forced periods is the intended "period setting", and whether the framework permits disabling period decomposition for the "none" ablation.
- UNCERTAINTY: whether multi-seed/statistical checks are feasible within the compute budget; they are designed as optional robustness layers so the core grid remains viable even without them.

The design is fully parameterized so that binding (K, {P}, mode) to the actual repo parameter names (when available) changes only the axis label, not the experimental logic, controls, or analysis.
